title: Differential timeout stitching experiment log
content:
Purpose:
This notebook-doc captures an exploratory run of a new scheduler idea: differential-timeout stitching. Goal is to reduce p95/p99 tail latency under mixed workloads (long-sequence generator + short-chat) while preserving throughput and avoiding starvation of low-cost short requests. This is intentionally rough — notes, configs, and early results.

Background and motivation:
- Continuous batching gives great throughput but suffers when request lengths and urgency differ. Current single-timeout policies either flush too early (low throughput) or too late (bad tail for short urgent requests).
- We hypothesize that per-tenant/request-class timeout "stitching" (maintain multiple concurrent flush horizons and pick earliest compatible flush for each inflight request) can keep throughput high while bounding short-request tails.

Terminology:
- stitch horizon: a scheduled flush point at a fixed deadline offset from a request's enqueue time.
- anchor class: small/urgent requests (<= 64 tokens) with tight SLOs.
- bulk class: generator/embedding-like long requests with loose SLOs.

Experiment plan:
1) Baseline: current hybrid-size-timeout policy (timeout=10ms, max-batch=64) on 4xA100 nodes, 16 workers. Collect 1M requests trace replay (mixed ratio anchor:bulk = 70:30).
2) Stitching v1: two horizons per worker: early=6ms (prefer anchors), late=30ms (bulk). Compatible batching allows mixing but anchor-tagged requests mark preference.
3) Stitching v2: adaptive early horizon (quantile-based): early = 1.5 * median inter-arrival anchor latency measured per shard, capped [3ms,10ms].
4) Fairness-cost: add linear penalty term for anchor waiting time into batch selection score, weight sweep over {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}.

Instrumentation and metrics collected:
- per-request: enqueue_time, flush_time, service_start, service_end, tokens_in, class_tag, batch_size_at_flush
- aggregates: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency for anchor and bulk separately, total tokens/sec, GPU-util, batch_size distribution, starved_count (requests delayed > 2*SLO)

Key results (summary):
- Baseline: anchor p95=42ms, p99=120ms; bulk p95=420ms; tokens/sec=52k; mean batch size=22.
- Stitching v1: anchor p95=18ms, p99=48ms; bulk p95=450ms; tokens/sec=49k; mean batch size=18. Early horizon shaved anchor tail by ~2.3x but small throughput drop.
- Stitching v2 (adaptive early): anchor p95=16ms, p99=36ms; bulk p95=460ms; tokens/sec=50k; mean batch size=19. Adaptive horizon preserved more throughput while improving anchors.
- Fairness-cost weight=0.5: anchor p99 reduced to 28ms, bulk p95 increased to 480ms, tokens/sec=47k. Slight throughput sacrifice traded for anchor fairness.

Observations and micro-insights:
- Mixing classes inside a batch causes KV-cache and attention fusion variance; some kernel launch overhead increased for mixed batches -> bulk p95 inflation. Consider two-path fast-path (pure anchor microbatch and mixed slow-path).
- Anchor starvation often occurs during microburst of bulk arrivals — adaptive early horizon that shortens on anchor pressure helps but requires per-shard telemetry to avoid oscillation. We saw a feedback loop when adaptation used raw recent inter-arrival quantiles; smoothing (EWMA alpha=0.2) stabilized.
- Stitching introduces bookkeeping (per-request horizon tags) but low mem overhead. More expensive is the logic in the coalescer: need fast decisions in hot path, so implemented horizon check as bitmask and precomputed compatible masks per queue slice.

Failure modes encountered:
- Edge-case: anchor requests re-tagged incorrectly when a retry comes back; caused anchor p99 spikes. Mitigation: idempotency guard and explicit retry-tag propagation.
- Oscillation: naive adaptive early horizon reacted to short-lived spikes, oscillating between 4ms and 12ms; smoothed EWMA and minimum dwell time (100ms) removed oscillation.

Detailed run notes (select traces):
- Trace 2024-11-08-11:12 (70:30) baseline replay: long tail correlated with batch-size collapse during a client-side synchronized burst. Microtrace shows 1 worker with 80% CPU GC stop-the-world pause -> inflated enqueue_time. Follow-up: add GC monitoring to SLO dashboards.
- Trace 2024-11-10-09:04 stitching-v2: anchor latencies stable, but mixed batches had 1.9x kernel-launch variance; filed PR #678 to expose kernel selection by mixed-batch shape.

Actionable next steps:
- Implement pure-anchor fast-path microbatches in the runtime to avoid mixed-batch kernel penalties. Benchmark expected uplift ~10% tokens/sec.
- Promote adaptive early horizon to production in a small canary: 5% of traffic, tenant-weighted, with rollback if p99_anchor > 50ms.
- Add per-shard EWMA telemetry pipeline for inter-arrival stats and tune dwell_time=100ms, alpha=0.2 by default.
- Run fairness weight grid: [0.1,0.25,0.5,0.75] across multiple mix ratios (80:20, 50:50, 30:70) to find robust operating point.

Open questions / discussion points:
- Is kernel-level optimization (separate attention kernels for short-prefix-heavy batches) more effective than scheduler complexity? Cost estimate: medium dev effort, high payoff for short-request SLOs.
- For Dedicated customers, do we expose stitching knobs or pick safe defaults? Risk: mis-config leads to throughput regressions. Proposal: expose as boolean + tenant class weights.
- Can we recycle KV-cache affinities to prefer bulk with same model/sequence-shape in late horizons? Might improve bulk p95.

Appendix (config snippets):
- worker.conf snippet:
  batcher.stitching.enabled=true
  batcher.stitching.early_ms=6
  batcher.stitching.late_ms=30
  batcher.stitching.adaptive=true
  batcher.stitching.adaptive.alpha=0.2
  batcher.fairness.weight=0.5

- quick note on reproducibility: replay harness used deterministic seeds, clients simulated jittered arrivals (Poisson + occasional synchronized bursts). All runs seeded and stored under s3://redwood-experiments/2024-11/timeout-stitching/

Notes-to-self: paste microtraces into a Confluence timeline, capture kernel profile flamegraphs, and schedule a sync with solutions-eng/benchmarks to discuss Dedicated default settings.

End of doc.
